content: 1. FOM (floor of mouth) reconstruction aims to close defects that communicate with the neck, thereby preventing the risk of blood vessel rupture caused by salivary contamination. The flap used must be of an appropriate width to avoid tethering the tip of the tongue to the FOM. Fasciocutaneous radial forearm free flaps are commonly used for FOM defect reconstruction. Recently, pedicled flaps, such as facial artery musculomucosal flaps, have gained popularity for addressing small or moderate FOM defects, offering excellent functional and aesthetic outcomes. 2. Buccal defect reconstruction focuses on preventing limitations in mouth opening, such as trismus, while preserving structural aesthetics. For cases involving significant muscle loss or buccal defects after resection of T2 or larger tumors, soft tissue flap reconstruction is recommended. Superficial buccal mucosal defects are typically treated with skin grafts. Radial forearm fasciocutaneous flaps are preferred for buccal mucosal defects, as they maintain the original open-mouth width and provide excellent functional outcomes. For through-and-through buccal defects, folded fasciocutaneous free flaps or flaps with dual perforating skin paddles are used to restore oral function and achieve acceptable cosmetic results. 3. Mandibular reconstruction for oral cancer defects primarily employs osteocutaneous free flaps, with the fibular free flap being the most commonly used option. This method is considered the gold standard due to its ability to provide superior functional and aesthetic outcomes. Computer-aided design (CAD) and manufacturing (CAM) technologies are increasingly being used to reduce surgical time and minimize errors during mandibular reconstruction. These technologies allow for precise planning, modeling, and execution of the reconstruction process. 4. Mandibular reconstruction is essential for restoring speech, swallowing, mastication, and the lower facial contour. Defects often involve a combination of skin, mucosa, and nerve tissues, necessitating a tailored approach to reconstruction. Autologous bone grafts should match the thickness and angulation of the mandible, while minimizing donor site morbidity. Osseointegrated implants can restore dentition, improving mastication and other functions. Soft tissue replacements must be thin and pliable to avoid impairing oral mobility. 5. The fibular free flap is the most frequently used osteocutaneous free flap for mandibular reconstruction, followed by the radial forearm, iliac crest, and scapular system flaps. Each option has specific advantages and disadvantages, such as bone length, skin paddle availability, pedicle length, and donor site morbidity. The fibular free flap is associated with the best quality of life outcomes and minimal donor site morbidity. 6. CAD/CAM technology has revolutionized mandibular reconstruction by enabling precise virtual surgical planning, rapid prototyping, and intraoperative navigation. This approach reduces ischemic and operating times while improving the accuracy of dental occlusion and orthognathic relationships. However, CAD/CAM has limitations, such as difficulty in estimating tumor margins and increased operating time, which may delay surgery. Despite these challenges, CAD/CAM is expected to play a larger role in mandibular reconstruction as its limitations are addressed. 7. Postoperative follow-up for oral cancer patients should include regular examinations for at least five years, with more frequent visits during the first two years due to the high risk of locoregional recurrence. Follow-up schedules should be individualized, taking into account the patient’s quality of life, nutritional status, speech and swallowing function, dental health, and other factors. Imaging studies, such as CT, MRI, and PET-CT, are recommended for detecting recurrences, metastases, and second primary tumors. 8. Thyroid function should be monitored in patients who have undergone radiation therapy to the head and neck, as hypothyroidism is a common complication. Thyroid function tests should be conducted twice yearly for the first five years and annually thereafter. Damage to the thyroid gland’s vascular supply during surgery or radiation-induced fibrosis are common causes of hypothyroidism. 9. Rehabilitation after oral cancer treatment should include speech therapy, swallowing rehabilitation, and shoulder rehabilitation. Swallowing and speech evaluations should be conducted within three months post-treatment, with early intervention being more beneficial. Shoulder dysfunction, often caused by spinal accessory nerve damage during neck dissection, should be addressed with progressive resistance training or other rehabilitation programs. 10. Lifestyle modifications are crucial for oral cancer survivors. Regular physical activity, a healthy diet, and abstinence from tobacco and alcohol are strongly recommended. Survivors should also maintain excellent oral hygiene and receive regular dental care to prevent complications such as dental caries, periodontal disease, and osteoradionecrosis. 11. Psychological support is essential for oral cancer survivors, who are at increased risk of depression, anxiety, and distress. Regular assessments using validated tools should be conducted, and counseling or pharmacotherapy should be offered as needed. Survivors may experience challenges related to body image, self-esteem, and social roles, which should be addressed through appropriate support and interventions. 12. Salvage surgery is a viable option for recurrent oral cavity cancer if resection is feasible. Elective neck dissection (END) may be considered for advanced recurrent tumors, while comprehensive neck dissection is recommended for cases with regional recurrence. The prognosis for salvage surgery depends on factors such as tumor stage, disease-free interval, and previous treatments.
